claims.claim: The International Labour Organization (19th International Conference of Labour Statisticians, 2013) defines work as comprising any activity performed by persons of any sex and age to produce goods or to provide services for use by others or for own use, irrespective of the activity's formal or informal character.

The ILO distinguishes five forms of work for measurement: employment work (performed for others in exchange for pay or profit), own-use production work (goods and services for own final use), unpaid trainee work, volunteer work (non-compulsory, without pay), and other work activities.

The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics defines the labor force as made up of the employed and the unemployed: people with jobs are employed; people who are jobless, looking for a job, and available for work are unemployed; people who are neither are not in the labor force.

BLS counts a person as employed if they did any work at all for pay or profit during the survey reference week — including all part-time and temporary work — or had a job but were not at work (vacation, illness, family obligations); unpaid family workers who worked 15 or more hours a week in a family business or farm also count as employed.

BLS counts a person as unemployed if they have no job, have actively looked for work in the prior four weeks, and are currently available for work; the survey covers people age 16 and over with no upper age limit and excludes people in institutions and on active duty in the Armed Forces.

OpenStax's Introduction to Sociology 3e describes automation of the workplace as replacing workers with technology: computers can be programmed to do many routine tasks faster and less expensively than people, and jobs like bookkeeping, clerical work, and repetitive assembly-line tasks lend themselves to automation.

OpenStax reports that the U.S. job market has become polarized: most employment opportunities sit at the lowest and highest levels, with fewer jobs for mid-level skills, and the fact that some positions are highly paid while others are not exemplifies the class system, an economic hierarchy.

OpenStax describes the American Dream as a cultural belief that studying hard, developing good work habits, and completing one's education lead to the opportunity to land a good job, long seen as the key to a successful life.
OpenStax introduces career inheritance: children tend to enter the same or similar occupations as their parents, a correlation demonstrated in research studies.

Pew Research Center found in February 2022 that roughly six-in-ten U.S. workers whose jobs can mainly be done from home (59%) were working from home all or most of the time — down from 71% in October 2020 but far above the 23% who teleworked frequently before the pandemic.

Britannica defines a gig as a part-time job performed by freelance workers for a limited amount of time; the word has historically been used by musicians and singers for engagements with a specific band or venue before moving on.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Does unpaid housework and care work count as 'work'?
positions: The ILO's broad definition includes own-use production work — goods and services produced for one's own final use, such as housework and home repairs — as a form of work.
The BLS labor-force measure counts only work for pay or profit (plus unpaid family workers in a family business or farm); a person doing only unpaid housework is classified as not in the labor force.
Both definitions are valid; they answer different questions — what counts as productive activity versus who official statistics count as working.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches both: the ILO definition for what work is as a social activity, and the BLS labor-force categories for who official statistics count as working, and it states the distinction plainly.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is gig work a new phenomenon or a relabeling of old arrangements?
positions: Britannica notes that a gig is a short-term freelance job and that the word comes from musicians' one-off engagements, so short-term work predates the internet.
Pew's surveys track how the arrangements people use to earn income are changing, including remote and platform-mediated work.
Whether gig work represents growth or a return to older, less secure arrangements is debated; that short-term freelance work exists as a category is not in dispute.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the definition and names gig work as one of the changes in how work is arranged, without taking a position on whether it is better or worse.
